figures.caption: Table 1: Notation used throughout the survey, following Prieto et al. (2026).

Figure 1: Feature directions in a two-dimensional hidden space and their relation to neuron responses. (a) Two features occupy the two neuron axes, so the encoding h = Wf gives each neuron one feature value. (b) A 45◦ rotation makes each neuron respond to both features while preserving the orthogonality of their directions and all encoded information. The rotated code therefore still fails clause 1 of Definition 2.1. (c) Five directions share the same two-dimensional space; the displayed nonzero inner products 〈wi, wj〉 show the overlap that is unavoidable when features outnumber dimensions.

Figure 2: Reconstruction and recovery in the one-dimensional codes of Definition 2.4. (a) For two Bernoulli(p) features, the dedicated code drops one feature and incurs risk p, whereas the antipodal code keeps both features and incurs 2p2. The antipodal error occurs when the two features fire together, an event of probability p2 on which the ReLU decoder errs on each feature. (b) Despite this error, the ReLU decoder achieves R2 = 1 − p 1−p → 1 as features become sparse, while the best linear decoder is capped at R2 = 1/2 for every p. For ε < 1 2 and small p, these features are therefore in non-linear superposition by Definition 2.2.
Table 2: Seven quantities used in discussions of capacity, in the notation of Table 1. Their input assumptions, recovery criteria, and resource counts differ.

Figure 3: Interference and linear-readout risk for overcomplete feature codes. (a) Arranging five features as a regular pentagon in two dimensions gives a unit-norm tight frame satisfying WW⊤ = (d/m) Im. (b) The off-diagonal entries of its Gram matrix give the pairwise interferences, whose squared sum meets the lower bound d(d−m)/m = 7.5 of Definition 3.2. (c) At width m = 16, the risk curves compare tied and untied linear readouts across overcompleteness ratios d/m, with risk measured in units of σ2. Random codes read with the tied readout V =W sit above the tied-readout lower bound d(d−m)/m. The optimal untied readout for a full-row-rank encoder attains d−m. The ratio d/m is attained by the two risks at a unit-norm tight frame, rather than by every random encoder (Definition 3.3).

Table 4: Computation bounds with their task and recovery conditions. In the all-pairs rows, d′ = ( d 2 ) . In the circuit row, n denotes the emulated circuit width, and the source provides a proof sketch with draft supporting material. The rows quantify over different tasks and resources; their widths do not form a hierarchy of readout strength.

Table 5: Sparse-autoencoder designs and their evaluated effects. The choices of coefficient estimation, sparsity control, hierarchy, and training target can interact. Reported improvements apply to the stated objectives and evaluations; identification of model features requires the additional conditions of Section 4.5.

Table 6: Recovery families compared by target, recovered object, and evaluation needs. The evidence categories in Section 2.5 identify what a test seeks to establish; belonging to a method family does not automatically establish a category. Section 8 examines the required references and controls.

Table 7: Evaluation metrics for recovered features. The last column records where a metric has been shown to disagree with another metric or with a supervised reference, not a general claim that it is invalid.
Table 8: Published dark-matter quantities. The three senses are not commensurable, and the row attributed to Engels et al. (2025b) is the one refereed entry.
Table 9: Reported compute and data for training and evaluating recovered dictionaries. Numbers are as published and are not normalized to common hardware or a common token count.
Table 10: Presuppositions used in dictionary learning, the failures they permit, and the evidence reported for each. A listed failure need not have been established in every setting.

Table 11: Work on superposition and feature recovery outside language models that we identified. The studies use different dictionaries, evaluation targets, and ground truth, so the rows are not comparable with one another.

Table 12: What became of the open questions stated by Elhage et al. (2022) and, for the superposition-relevant part of a much longer list, by Sharkey et al. (2025). Of fifty questions assessed, seventeen are displayed: all six with negative findings, all three reformulated questions, both answered questions, three partly answered questions, and three open questions. The thirty-three omitted questions comprise twenty-eight partly answered and five open questions. Verdicts summarize the evidence in the analyzed settings.
